title: Browser Capability APIs
description: Permissions, device capabilities, clipboard, notifications, observation, and page visibility with progressive enhancement and cleanup.
learningOutcomes: Request sensitive capabilities only in response to a clear user action and explain denial/failure states.
Use geolocation and clipboard APIs with feature checks, asynchronous error handling, and cleanup.
Treat notifications and battery data as optional capabilities with user consent and compatibility limits.
Use ResizeObserver and Page Visibility without creating feedback loops or unnecessary background work.
Request notification permission after user intent and handle desktop/mobile display paths with an in-page fallback.

blocks.text: Browser capabilities are conditional, not guaranteed

A browser API is a request to use a capability under several gates: the API may be absent, the page may not be a secure context, the user may deny permission, an embedding policy may block it, or the operation may fail at runtime. Treat each gate as a normal branch in the interface—not as an exceptional browser quirk. Ask only when the user understands the benefit, provide a useful fallback, and never make a sensitive capability the only way to complete a task.

items: Feature detection answers whether an API is exposed; it does not prove permission or successful operation.
Secure context (normally HTTPS, with localhost exceptions) is required by several sensitive APIs.
Permission prompts should follow an explicit, contextual user action; prompting on page load surprises people and may be blocked by browsers.
Permissions Policy can further restrict APIs in embedded documents; test the deployed origin and iframe configuration, not only localhost.

blocks.text: Geolocation: permission, error states, and watch cleanup

steps.title: Keep the request user-initiated
steps.explanation: The click is the point where the user asks to use location. Explain the benefit before this action; do not prompt immediately on page load.

steps.title: Check support and report failure
steps.explanation: The interface may not expose geolocation. A supported call can still fail because permission is denied, the position is unavailable, or the timeout elapses.

steps.title: Choose one reading or a live watch deliberately
steps.explanation: watchPosition repeatedly invokes callbacks and returns an ID. The guard prevents duplicate watches; maximumAge permits a cached fix and timeout bounds waiting, but neither guarantees accuracy.

steps.title: Stop resources you no longer need
steps.explanation: Call clearWatch with the returned ID when the view is disposed or the user stops sharing, then clear the stored ID. For a one-time location, use getCurrentPosition instead.

blocks.title: Location is sensitive data
blocks.text: Request the least precise data the feature needs, explain retention and sharing, and avoid logging coordinates. A permission grant is not consent to upload or retain location indefinitely. Secure context and Permissions Policy restrictions can prevent the API from working.

blocks.prompt: A map panel unmounts while watchPosition is active. What should cleanup do?

options.text: Nothing; the browser stops every geolocation watch when a component disappears.
options.feedback: The browser API is not tied automatically to a UI component lifecycle; the watch can continue.

options.text: Call clearWatch with the ID returned by watchPosition.
options.feedback: Correct. Retain the watch ID and clear it when the feature is no longer active.

options.text: Call navigator.permissions.query and assume it cancels the reading.
options.feedback: Permission inspection does not stop a watch; cancellation uses clearWatch.

options.text: Reload the page so the permission prompt appears again.
options.feedback: Reloading is disruptive and does not express lifecycle cleanup.

blocks.explanation: The application owns the watch lifecycle. Cleanup stops repeated callbacks and prevents stale UI updates or unnecessary device work.

steps.title: Start from a direct user gesture
steps.explanation: The click handler provides clear intent. Clipboard permissions and user-activation requirements vary across browsers, especially for reads.

steps.title: Feature-detect the exact method
steps.explanation: The Clipboard API is exposed in secure contexts and may be unavailable. Optional chaining checks the method, then a manual fallback keeps the task possible.

steps.title: Await and handle rejection
steps.explanation: writeText returns a promise. Permission, focus, policy, or platform restrictions can reject it, so report success only after it resolves.

blocks.title: Do not treat clipboard access as silent background work
blocks.text: Reading clipboard contents is more privacy-sensitive than writing a value the user asked to copy. Browser requirements differ; request reads only for an explicit paste-related action and handle denial. Avoid legacy execCommand-based examples except when deliberately documenting compatibility fallback.
Request and show notifications with a safe fallback

Ask for permission only after an explicit user action and only in a secure context. Permission may be `granted`, `denied`, or `default`; denial or unsupported APIs must leave an in-page status path usable. On most mobile browsers, `new Notification()` throws; use an available `ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification()` for persistent notifications, and catch display failures rather than claiming success. This is a capability example, not a push subscription or background delivery implementation.

steps.title: Detect availability before using the API
steps.explanation: Both the button and status area are optional page elements. Check API support and secure context before touching `Notification`; if unavailable, explain the in-page alternative.

steps.title: Request permission only after a click
steps.explanation: Request permission only when the user activates the button. Preserve granted/denied/default distinctions and handle a rejected permission promise; do not report that a notification was shown yet.

steps.title: Prefer the service-worker path when registered
steps.explanation: A registration can show persistent notifications and is the required route for most mobile browsers. The constructor is only a fallback when no registration is available; display can still fail, so handle the error and keep the in-page status.

steps.title: Attach and remove a stable click handler
steps.explanation: The explicit button click is the permission user gesture. `disposeNotificationFeature()` removes the exact function reference so a disposed feature does not retain the handler.

blocks.prompt: When is the best time to call Notification.requestPermission()?

options.text: Automatically as soon as every page loads.
options.feedback: Unexpected permission prompts harm trust and browsers may suppress them.

options.text: After a user chooses an explained opt-in action, with a fallback if permission is denied or unsupported.
options.feedback: Correct. Permission should be contextual and opt-in; notification support is not universal.

options.text: After silently creating a Notification object.
options.feedback: Displaying notifications requires permission; constructing one does not replace the permission flow.

options.text: Only from a Service Worker, so a page never needs permission.
options.feedback: A service worker can show notifications in supported flows, but permission is still required.

blocks.explanation: Notifications display outside the page and require explicit origin permission. Ask only after explaining what the user will receive, and preserve an in-page alternative.

steps.title: Observe the element, not just the viewport
steps.explanation: A component can resize because its container or neighboring layout changes even when the window size does not. ResizeObserver reports element box changes.

steps.title: Read the measured size and derive presentation
steps.explanation: The content box size is preferred when available; contentRect is a compatibility fallback. The threshold is a product decision and should avoid jitter near the boundary if necessary.

steps.title: Avoid observer feedback loops
steps.explanation: This callback changes only a class for styling. If callback writes change the observed dimensions, it can trigger repeated notifications; make the transformation converge or defer carefully.

steps.title: Disconnect on teardown
steps.explanation: Stop observing when the element/view is gone. Disconnect releases every observed target owned by this observer.

steps.title: Pause work while the page is hidden
steps.explanation: Pause expensive or user-invisible activity when the document is hidden. The play() promise can reject due to autoplay policy, so show a manual-play fallback instead of hiding the failure.

steps.title: Register the same named callback
steps.explanation: The named onVisibilityChange function is registered and later removed by the same reference; the initial call handles current page state before an event fires.

steps.title: Remove the listener on teardown
steps.explanation: Cleanup removes the exact registered callback. A new anonymous arrow would be a different function and would leave the original listener attached.

blocks.title: Battery data is optional and not broadly available
blocks.text: Battery Status API support is limited, requires a secure context, and is not exposed in Web Workers. Feature-detect it and use it only as a progressive enhancement; never block core functionality or infer a person's behavior from battery level.

blocks.title: Build a capability-aware share panel
blocks.context: A lesson page offers a Copy link button and an optional “use my location” shortcut. Implement them so every path still works when browser capabilities or permission are unavailable.
instructions: Implement the click handler for Copy link with feature detection, awaited success, and a manual-copy fallback.
Add a separate location button that explains why location is useful before requesting a one-time position.
Render distinct messages for unsupported, permission denied, timeout/unavailable, success, and clipboard rejection.
Do not request location or notifications on page load; do not send or persist coordinates.
Add cleanup if you choose watchPosition instead of the required one-time getCurrentPosition.
Implement optional notifications only from a dedicated user gesture; preserve an in-page update fallback for denied/unsupported APIs and prefer service-worker showNotification on mobile.
requirements: Check `navigator.clipboard?.writeText` and call it only after the user's copy action.
Use `getCurrentPosition` for a one-time shortcut; request only on the location button click.
Keep all failure states actionable and avoid exposing precise coordinates beyond the UI requirement.
Keep optional APIs from blocking the rest of the share panel.
Notification permission is not requested during setup; denied/unsupported/display-failed paths keep the in-page status usable.
hints: The browser may expose the object but permission can still reject the call.
Check GeolocationPositionError codes, but do not assume every device returns a useful fix.
A manual-copy instruction is a real fallback, not a swallowed exception.
If you switch to watchPosition, store its ID and clear it when the user stops.
The Notification constructor fails on most mobile browsers; use an active ServiceWorkerRegistration when available, but still catch the display promise.
successCriteria: No prompt is requested during initial page setup.
Clipboard success is shown only after the promise resolves.
Unsupported and rejected clipboard cases have a manual alternative.
Location is requested only from the location button and failures are explained.
No location is uploaded or persisted by the implementation.
Each action leaves the other capability usable when unavailable.
Notification permission is requested only from a user action; desktop/mobile display paths and in-page fallback are handled without false success feedback.
